Photo taken at a Community Resilience Center Retreat in Corpus Christi, TX (2026)





Photo taken in Hattiesburg, MS during an EPA Brownfield Site Assessment “tank yank.”




I’m a social scientist, resilience researcher, and data nerd interested in what happens when environmental risk meets the places people actually live.
My work combines social science, spatial analysis, and community resilience. I use R, GIS, and real-world data to study flooding, housing, insurance, and vulnerability, and turn that information into something communities can actually use.
I earned my Ph.D. in Sociology studying inequities in disaster impacts and recovery, and now work on applied resilience projects across coastal Mississippi. At the heart of my work is a love for using data to answer questions that matter to real places and real people.

title: Hurrican Ida: Wind & Storm Surge Attribution Analysis
text:
Overview
This interdisciplinary project with LSU, the National Center for Atmospheric Research, and The Water Institute examined Hurricane Ida’s impacts under changing climate conditions.
My role was to integrate modeled wind and storm-surge damage estimates with demographic data and to analyze the distribution of climate change attributable impacts across different populations and communities.
Code to create the statistics, figures, and maps from this project can be found here.

title: Climate Change & Federal Aid Dispersements
text:
Overview
This was an interdisciplinary effort to assess the relationship between climate change attributable damages and federal disaster assistance.
I integrated modeled flood damages with FEMA NFIP paid claims and Individual Assistance payouts, applied spatial lag regression models to estimate both direct and spatial spillover effects of attributable damages, and created maps to visualize the relationship.
Results indicate that while both attributable and non-attributable flood damages were associated with federal aid, climate change attributable damages generally had larger effect sizes, particularly for Individual Assistance.

title: Bay St. Louis | CRS Activity 510
text:
Overview
The project team is supporting the City of Bay St. Louis in earning credit under Community Rating System Activity 510.
My role in this project is to determine which areas are most exposed to different types of flooding, develop maps and other visuals, analyze flood insurance and claims data, and write sections of the plans.

title: D’Iberville, MS | CRS Activity 610
text:
Overview
The project team supported the City of D’Iberville in developing a flood response plan for Community Rating System (CRS) Activity 610.
I used R to calculate the proportion of buildings exposed to coastal and riverine flooding, then used ArcGIS to map flood extent, depth, and exposure.
I also participated in stakeholder meetings to ensure that the CRS scenarios aligned with those established in the community’s flood planning and forecasting protocols.



Project Work

Flood hazard and exposure mapping

Hurricane Category 1 and 3 Storm Surge
Minor, Moderate, and Major Riverine Flood Stages

Geocoding and mapping critical facilities
Stakeholder engagement and plan writing

Data

Coastal scenarios: SLOSH
Riverine scenarios: NOAA Riverine Flood Inundation

title: Mapping Flood Insurance Participation
text:
In this project, I used OpenFEMA data to map the distribution of National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) coverage and identify areas with relatively low levels of participation.
The map below presents two measures of policy participation: the total number of effective residential NFIP policies and residential policies normalized by the number of housing units. Mapping both measures distinguishes places with large numbers of policies simply because they contain more households from places where flood insurance is more prevalent relative to the local housing stock.






Data & Methods: OpenFEMA NFIP Policies · U.S. Census/ACS housing data · R · sf · leaflet · rfema
All code used to extract OpenFEMA NFIP policy data and American Community Survey estimates, process the data, and create this map is available on GitHub here.

title: Waveland, MS | CRS Activity 510
text:
Overview
The project team supported the City of Waveland in developing an Activity 510 floodplain management plan, substantial damage management plan, and repetitive loss area analysis for FEMA’s Community Rating System.
My role was to analyze the vulnerability of people and structures to a variety of flood hazards, including high tide flooding, storm surge, stormwater flooding, and the 100- and 500-year floods, and to identify which areas had the highest NFIP policy participation and paid claims. The analysis identified areas of greatest concern and will inform local floodplain management priorities.

#load packages
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, duckdb, tigris)

#connect to the database 
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

# query data for your area of interest (i.e., update the county code for your FIPs)
nfip_policy_raw <- dbGetQuery(con, "
                   SELECT *
                   FROM read_csv_auto('data/FimaNfipPoliciesV2.csv')
                   WHERE countyCode = 01097
                   ") 

# make variables with different resident types (optional)
single_family <- c(1, 11, 14)
two_to_four_family = c(2, 12)
multi_family <- c(3, 13, 15, 16)
non_residential <- c(4, 6, 17, 18, 19)

#set end date
end_date <- as.Date("2026-01-17") 

# tidy the data and make new variables
nfip_policy <- 
  nfip_policy_raw %>%
  transmute(
    across(c(policyEffectiveDate,
             policyTerminationDate,
             cancellationDateOfFloodPolicy), ~ as.Date(.x)), 
    countyCode,
    nfipCommunityName,
    nfipRatedCommunityNumber,
    
    effective = ifelse( #indicates whether the policy is effective
      policyEffectiveDate <= end_date &
      policyTerminationDate >= end_date &
        (cancellationDateOfFloodPolicy >= end_date |
           is.na(cancellationDateOfFloodPolicy)), 1, 0
    ),
    
    #create residence type variables
    single_family = ifelse(occupancyType %in% single_family, 1, 0),
    two_to_four_family = ifelse(occupancyType %in% two_to_four_family, 1, 0),
    multi_family = ifelse(occupancyType %in% multi_family, 1, 0),
    non_residential = ifelse(occupancyType %in% non_residential, 1, 0),
    occupancy_type = case_when(
      single_family == 1 ~ "Single Family",
      two_to_four_family == 1 ~ "2-4 Family",
      multi_family == 1 ~ "All Other Residential",
      non_residential == 1 ~ "Non-Residential"
    ) %>%
      factor(levels = c("Single Family", "2-4 Family", 
                        "All Other Residential", "Non-Residential")),
    
    #coverage amount variables
    totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy,
    totalBuildingInsuranceCoverage,
    totalContentsInsuranceCoverage,
    total_coverage = 
      totalBuildingInsuranceCoverage + 
      totalContentsInsuranceCoverage
  ) %>%
  filter(
    effective == 1 &
    countyCode == "01097" &
    nfipRatedCommunityNumber == "220139" #need to update !
    )

# create a table broken apart by residence type
nfip_policy %>%
  group_by(occupancy_type) %>% 
  summarize(
    number_policies = n(),
    total_premium = sum(totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy), 
    insurance_in_force = sum(total_coverage),
    .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      occupancy_type = "Total",
      number_policies = nrow(nfip_policy),
      total_premium = sum(nfip_policy$totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy), 
      insurance_in_force = sum(nfip_policy$total_coverage)
      )
    ) %>%
  transmute(
    'Occupancy Type' = occupancy_type,
    'Number of Policies in Force' = comma(number_policies),
    'Total Premium' = comma(total_premium),
    'Insurance in Force' = comma(insurance_in_force)
    )
